# Research Advances in Code Agents and Red-teaming

## Abstract

The rapid advancement of code agents—AI systems capable of generating, executing, and debugging code autonomously—has revolutionized software development and automated coding workflows. However, the increasing capabilities of code agents have also introduced significant security and safety concerns. This paper provides a comprehensive review of research advances in code agents and red-teaming methodologies. We examine recent benchmarks and frameworks designed to evaluate the safety, trustworthiness, and security of code agents through systematic red-teaming approaches. We discuss the emergence of dedicated red-teaming agents that automatically identify vulnerabilities and risky behaviors in code-generating systems. Our review highlights critical gaps in current methodologies and proposes directions for future research in building safer, more reliable code agent systems.

## Introduction

Code agents represent a transformative class of AI systems that can autonomously write, execute, and debug code. Powered by large language models (LLMs), these agents have shown remarkable capabilities in tasks ranging from simple code completion to complex software engineering workflows involving multiple reasoning steps, tool use, and iterative debugging [1]. As code agents become increasingly integrated into production environments—from automated software testing pipelines to AI-assisted coding assistants in development tools—their safety and reliability have become paramount concerns.

The dual-use nature of code agents presents unique security challenges. On one hand, they enable unprecedented productivity gains and automation of repetitive coding tasks. On the other hand, their ability to generate and execute arbitrary code introduces potential attack vectors, including the execution of malicious payloads, data exfiltration, and system compromise. These risks are particularly pronounced when code agents operate in untrusted environments or when their outputs are executed without adequate security safeguards.

Red-teaming—the process of systematically probing systems for vulnerabilities—has emerged as a critical methodology for evaluating and improving code agent safety. Unlike traditional penetration testing, red-teaming for AI systems requires understanding both the technical capabilities of the models and the adversarial scenarios they may encounter in real-world deployments. Recent research has focused on developing automated red-teaming frameworks that can efficiently discover vulnerabilities in code agents through systematic exploration of their behavior space.

This paper reviews the current state of research in code agents and red-teaming, organized as follows. Section 2 surveys related work, including recent red-teaming frameworks specifically designed for code agents, comprehensive benchmarks for evaluating code agent safety, trustworthiness assessments of generative models, and foundational deep learning architectures that enable these capabilities. Section 3 discusses key research advances and methodologies. Section 4 outlines challenges and future directions. Section 5 concludes the paper.

## Related Work

The field of code agent safety and red-teaming has seen rapid growth in recent years. Below we discuss several foundational and recent works that have shaped the current research landscape.

**RedCodeAgent: Automatic Red-teaming Agent against Diverse Code Agents.** Guo et al. [2] introduced RedCodeAgent, a novel framework for automatically red-teaming diverse code agents. Unlike manual security testing approaches, RedCodeAgent employs an automated agent that systematically generates adversarial prompts and evaluates the safety of target code agents. The framework is designed to identify a wide range of vulnerabilities including malicious code generation, unsafe code execution patterns, and security bypass attempts. Their work demonstrates the effectiveness of automated red-teaming in uncovering safety issues that might be missed by conventional testing methods, particularly across different code agent architectures and capabilities.

**RedCode: Risky Code Execution and Generation Benchmark for Code Agents.** Building on the need for standardized evaluation, Guo et al. [3] presented RedCode, a comprehensive benchmark specifically designed to assess the safety of code agents. RedCode focuses on evaluating both the generation and execution of risky code, covering scenarios such as malware generation, security exploit code, privacy violations, and other potentially harmful outputs. The benchmark provides a structured framework for measuring code agent safety across multiple dimensions, enabling systematic comparison of different agents' safety profiles. Their evaluation reveals significant safety concerns across existing code agent systems and highlights the urgency of developing more robust safety mechanisms.

**DecodingTrust: A Comprehensive Assessment of Trustworthiness in GPT Models.** The broader context of AI trustworthiness has been addressed in DecodingTrust [4], which provides a comprehensive assessment of trustworthiness in generative pre-trained transformer models. While not specifically focused on code agents, this work establishes foundational evaluation methodologies for trustworthiness that are directly applicable to code agent safety. The framework evaluates models across multiple trustworthiness dimensions including harmful content generation, bias, fairness, robustness, and privacy. Their extensive evaluation of various GPT model families provides insights into the trustworthiness properties that are essential for any AI system, including code agents, that interact with users and execute code in production environments.

**Deep Residual Learning for Image Recognition.** The architectural foundations that enable modern code agents trace back to advances in deep learning. He et al. [5] introduced residual learning, a breakthrough architecture that enabled the training of substantially deeper neural networks. By reformulating layers to learn residual functions with reference to layer inputs, residual networks (ResNets) addressed the vanishing gradient problem that previously limited network depth. This architectural innovation became a cornerstone for the development of large language models, including the transformer-based architectures that power contemporary code agents. The ability to train very deep networks through residual connections has been critical to achieving the model capabilities that make modern code agents so powerful—and so potentially dangerous if deployed without adequate safety measures.

These works collectively establish the foundation for current research in code agent safety and red-teaming. The automated red-teaming frameworks demonstrate the effectiveness of systematic vulnerability discovery, benchmarks provide standardized evaluation methodologies, trustworthiness assessments offer broader evaluation frameworks, and foundational deep learning research enables the underlying model capabilities.

## Conclusion

The field of code agents has advanced rapidly, offering unprecedented capabilities for automated software development and coding assistance. However, the security and safety implications of these powerful systems necessitate rigorous evaluation and continuous improvement. Through the review of recent research, we have highlighted several key advances: automated red-teaming frameworks that can efficiently discover vulnerabilities, comprehensive benchmarks for standardized safety evaluation, trustworthiness assessment methodologies applicable to code agents, and the deep learning foundations that enable these systems.

Several challenges remain. Current red-teaming approaches often focus on known vulnerability categories and may miss novel attack vectors. Benchmark coverage, while improving, still cannot capture the full spectrum of potential security scenarios. Additionally, the evaluation of code agents in realistic, multi-step workflows requires more sophisticated testing frameworks. Future work should focus on developing more comprehensive and adaptive red-teaming methodologies, creating benchmarks that cover a wider range of safety scenarios, and integrating safety evaluation directly into the code agent development lifecycle.

As code agents become increasingly prevalent in software development workflows, continued research into their safety and security is not just beneficial—it is essential for the responsible deployment of these transformative technologies.

## Introduction

Code agents represent a transformative class of AI systems that can autonomously write, execute, and debug code. Powered by large language models (LLMs), these agents have shown remarkable capabilities in tasks ranging from simple code completion to complex software engineering workflows involving multiple reasoning steps, tool use, and iterative debugging [1]. As code agents become increasingly integrated into production environments—from automated software testing pipelines to AI-assisted coding assistants in development tools—their safety and reliability have become paramount concerns.

The dual-use nature of code agents presents unique security challenges. On one hand, they enable unprecedented productivity gains and automation of repetitive coding tasks. On the other hand, their ability to generate and execute arbitrary code introduces potential attack vectors, including the execution of malicious payloads, data exfiltration, and system compromise. These risks are particularly pronounced when code agents operate in untrusted environments or when their outputs are executed without adequate security safeguards.

Red-teaming—the process of systematically probing systems for vulnerabilities—has emerged as a critical methodology for evaluating and improving code agent safety. Unlike traditional penetration testing, red-teaming for AI systems requires understanding both the technical capabilities of the models and the adversarial scenarios they may encounter in real-world deployments. Recent research has focused on developing automated red-teaming frameworks that can efficiently discover vulnerabilities in code agents through systematic exploration of their behavior space.

This paper reviews the current state of research in code agents and red-teaming, organized as follows. Section 2 surveys related work, including recent red-teaming frameworks specifically designed for code agents, comprehensive benchmarks for evaluating code agent safety, trustworthiness assessments of generative models, and foundational deep learning architectures that enable these capabilities.
